{{smaller|'''Churching of women.''' See ''church'', ''v.''—'''Lawful woman.''' See ''lawful''.—'''Married Woman’s Act,''' the name under which are known a number of statutes, both in Great Britain and in the United States (dating about 1850 and thereafter), by which the common-law disabilities of married women as to contracts, property, and rights of action have by successive steps been nearly all removed.—'''Old woman’s tooth.''' Same as ''router-plane'' (which see, under ''router'').—'''Old-woman’s tree.''' See ''Quiina''.—'''Single woman.''' See ''single''.—'''The scarlet woman.''' See ''scarlet''.—'''To be tied to a woman’s apron-strings.''' See ''apron-string''.—'''To make an honest woman of.''' See ''honest''.—'''To play the woman,''' to give way to tenderness or pity; weep.—'''Wise woman.''' See ''wise''<sup>1</sup>.—'''Woman of the town,''' a prostitute.—'''Woman of the world.''' (''a''†) A married woman. See ''to go to the world'', under ''world''. (''b'') A woman experienced in the ways of the world; a woman engrossed in society or fashionable life.}}

'''woman†''' (wu̇m′ạn), ''v. t.'' [< ''woman'', ''n.''] '''1.''' To act the part of a woman: with an indefinite ''it.''
{{smaller block|<poem>
This day I should
Haue seene my daughter Siluia how she would
Haue ''womand it.''
</poem>
{{right|''Daniel'', Hymen’s Triumph, iii. 2.}}}}
'''2.''' To cause to act like a woman; subdue to weakness like a woman.
{{smaller block|<poem>
I have felt so many quirks of joy and grief
That the first face of neither, on the start,
Can ''woman'' me unto ’t.
</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', All’s Well, iii. 2. 53.}}}}
'''3.''' To unite to, or accompany by, a woman.
{{smaller block|<poem>
I do attend here on the general;
And think it no addition, nor my wish,
To have him see me ''woman’d''.
</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Othello, iii. 4. 195.}}}}
'''4.''' To call (a person) “woman” in an abusive way.
{{smaller block|She called her another time fat-face, and ''womaned'' her most violently. {{right|''Richardson'', Pamela, II. 268. (''Davies''.)}}}}

'''womanhead†''' (wu̇m′an-hed), ''n.'' [< ME. ''wommanhede''; < ''woman'' + ''-head.''] The state or condition of a woman; womanhood.
{{smaller block|<poem>The quene anon, for verray ''wommanhede,''
Gan for to wepe. {{right|''Chaucer'', Knight’s Tale, l. 890.}}</poem>}}
{{smaller block|<poem>I shall as now do more for you
Than longeth to ''Womanhede.''</poem>
{{right|''The Nut-Brown Maid.''}}}}

'''womanhood''' (wu̇m′ạn-hu̇d), ''n.'' [< ME. *''wommanhod''; < ''woman'' + ''-hood.'' Cf. ''womanhead.''] '''1.''' Womanly state, character, or qualities; the state of being a woman.

'''womb-passage''' (wöm′pas″ạ̄j), ''n.'' The vagina. See cut under ''peritoneum.''

'''womb-pipe†''', ''n.'' Same as ''womb-passage.'' ''Cotgrave.''

<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="transcriber" />{{RunningHeader|woman|6961|womb-pipe}}</noinclude>{{nop}}{{smaller block|Pray, Mr. Neverout, hold your tongue for once, if it be possible; one would think you were a ''woman'' in man’s cloaths, by your prating.
{{right|''Swift'', Polite Conversation, iii.}}}}
{{smaller block|''Woman'' seems to differ from man in mental disposition, chiefly in her greater tenderness and less selfishness; and this holds good even with savages.
{{right|''Darwin'', Descent of Man, II. 311.}}}}

'''2.''' The qualities which characterize womanhood; tenderness; gentleness; also, when used of a man, effeminacy; weakness.
{{smaller block|<poem>But that my eyes
Have more of ''woman'' in ’em than my heart,
I would not weep.</poem>
{{right|''Beau. and Fl.'', King and No King, iv. 4.}}}}

'''3.''' A female attendant on a person of rank (used in such a connection as to show the special sense intended).
{{smaller block|Take it to oon of youre moste secrete ''woman'', and bid hir deliuer it to the firste man that she fyndeth at the issue of the halle.
{{right|''Merlin'' (E. E. T. S.), i. 90.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Sir Thomas Bullen’s daughter —
The Viscount Rochford — one of her highness’ ''women''.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Hen. VIII., i. 4. 93.}}}}
{{smaller block|'''Churching of women.''' See ''church'', ''v.''—'''Lawful woman.''' See ''lawful''.—'''Married Woman’s Act,''' the name under which are known a number of statutes, both in Great Britain and in the United States (dating about 1850 and thereafter), by which the common-law disabilities of married women as to contracts, property, and rights of action have by successive steps been nearly all removed.—'''Old woman’s tooth.''' Same as ''router-plane'' (which see, under ''router'').—'''Old-woman’s tree.''' See ''Quiina''.—'''Single woman.''' See ''single''.—'''The scarlet woman.''' See ''scarlet''.—'''To be tied to a woman’s apron-strings.''' See ''apron-string''.—'''To make an honest woman of.''' See ''honest''.—'''To play the woman,''' to give way to tenderness or pity; weep.—'''Wise woman.''' See ''wise''<sup>1</sup>.—'''Woman of the town,''' a prostitute.—'''Woman of the world.''' (''a''†) A married woman. See ''to go to the world'', under ''world''. (''b'') A woman experienced in the ways of the world; a woman engrossed in society or fashionable life.}}

'''woman†''' (wu̇m′ạn), ''v. t.''   [< ''woman'', ''n.'']   '''1.''' To act the part of a woman: with an indefinite ''it.''
{{smaller block|<poem>
This day I should
Haue seene my daughter Siluia how she would
Haue ''womand it.''
</poem>
{{right|''Daniel'', Hymen’s Triumph, iii. 2.}}}}
'''2.''' To cause to act like a woman; subdue to weakness like a woman.
{{smaller block|<poem>
I have felt so many quirks of joy and grief
That the first face of neither, on the start,
Can ''woman'' me unto ’t.
</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', All’s Well, iii. 2. 53.}}}}
'''3.''' To unite to, or accompany by, a woman.
{{smaller block|<poem>
I do attend here on the general;
And think it no addition, nor my wish,
To have him see me ''woman’d''.
</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Othello, iii. 4. 195.}}}}
'''4.''' To call (a person) “woman” in an abusive way.
{{smaller block|She called her another time fat-face, and ''womaned'' her most violently. {{right|''Richardson'', Pamela, II. 268. (''Davies''.)}}}}

'''woman-body''' (wům′a̤n-bod″i), ''n.'' A woman: used disparagingly or in self-depreciation. [Scotch.]
{{smaller block|It was an awkward thing for a ''woman-body'' to be standing among bundles o’ barkened leather her lane.
{{right|''Scott'', Heart of Mid-Lothian, x.}}}}

'''woman-born''' (wům′a̤n-bôrn), ''a.'' Born of woman.   ''Cowper'', Charity, l. 181.

'''woman-built''' (wům′a̤n-bilt), ''a.'' Built by women.
{{smaller block|A new-world Babel, ''woman-built.''
{{right|''Tennyson'', Princess, iv.}}}}

'''womanfully''' (wům′a̤n-fůl-i), ''adv.''   [< ''woman'' + ''-ful'' + ''-ly''<sup>2</sup>.]   Like a woman: a word humorously employed to correspond with ''manfully.''
{{smaller block|For near fourscore years she fought her fight ''womanfully.'' {{right|''Thackeray'', Newcomes, ii.}}}}
{{smaller block|Anne alone . . . stood up by her father ''womanfully'', and put her arm through his.
{{right|''Mrs. Oliphant'', Poor Gentleman, xlvi.}}}}

'''woman-grown''' (wům′a̤n-grōn), ''a.'' Grown to womanhood.   ''Tennyson'', Aylmer’s Field.

'''woman-guard''' (wům′a̤n-gärd), ''n.'' A guard of women.
{{smaller block|The Princess with her monstrous ''woman-guard.''
{{right|''Tennyson'', Princess, iv.}}}}

'''woman-hater''' (wům′a̤n-hā″tėr), ''n.'' One who has an aversion to women in general; a misogynist.
{{smaller block|This Coarseness [toward women] does not alwaies come from Clowns and ''Women-haters'', but from Persons of Figure, neither singular nor ill Bred.
{{right|''Jeremy Collier'', Short View (ed. 1698), p. 171.}}}}

'''womanhead†''' (wu̇m′an-hed), ''n.''   [< ME. ''wommanhede''; < ''woman'' + ''-head.'']   The state or condition of a woman; womanhood.
{{smaller block|<poem>The quene anon, for verray ''wommanhede,''
Gan for to wepe. {{right|''Chaucer'', Knight’s Tale, l. 890.}}</poem>}}
{{smaller block|<poem>I shall as now do more for you
Than longeth to ''Womanhede.''</poem>
{{right|''The Nut-Brown Maid.''}}}}

'''womanhood''' (wu̇m′ạn-hu̇d), ''n.''   [< ME. *''wommanhod''; < ''woman'' + ''-hood.'' Cf. ''womanhead.'']   '''1.''' Womanly state, character, or qualities; the state of being a woman. {{smaller block|Setting thy ''womanhood'' aside.
{{right|''Shak.'', 1 Hen. IV., iii. 3. 139.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Her ''womanhood''
In its meridian.</poem>
{{right|''Byron'', Don Juan, ix. 71.}}}}
'''2.''' Women collectively; womankind.

'''womanish''' (wu̇m′ạn-ish), ''a.''   [< ''woman'' + ''-ish''<sup>1</sup>.]   Pertaining to, characteristic of, or suitable for women; feminine; effeminate: often used in a disparaging or reproachful sense when said of men: as, ''womanish'' ways; a ''womanish'' voice; ''womanish'' fears.
{{smaller block|<poem>Tho wordes and tho ''wommannishe'' thynges,
She herde hem right as though she thennes.</poem>
{{right|''Chaucer'', Troilus, iv. 694.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>In what a shadow, or deep pit of darkness,
Doth ''womanish'' and fearful mankind live!</poem>
{{right|''Webster'', Duchess of Malfi, v. 5.}}}}
{{smaller block|He conceals, under a rough air and distant behaviour, a bleeding compassion and ''womanish'' tenderness.
{{right|''Steele'', Spectator, No. 346.}}}}
='''Syn.''' ''Female, Effeminate'', etc. See ''feminine''.

'''womanishly''' (wu̇m′ạn-ish-li), ''adv.'' In a womanish manner; effeminately.
{{smaller block|The people weare long haire, in combing whereof they are ''womanishly'' curious, these hoping by their lockes to be carried into heauen.
{{right|''Purchas'', Pilgrimage, p. 445.}}}}

'''womanishness''' (wu̇m′ạn-ish-nes), ''n.'' The state or character of being womanish.
{{smaller block|Effeminacy and ''womanishness'' of heart.
{{right|''Hammond'', Works, IV. 567.}}}}

'''womanize†''' (wu̇m′ạn-īz), ''v. t.''; pret. and pp. ''womanized'', ppr. ''womanizing''.   [< ''woman'' + ''-ize''.]   To make effeminate; make womanish; soften. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|This effeminate love of a woman doth so ''womanize'' a man.{{right|''Sir P. Sidney'', Arcadia, i.}}}}

'''womankind''' (wu̇m′an-kīnd′), ''n.''   [Also ''women-kind''; < ''woman'' + ''-kind''; contrasted with ''mankind''.]   '''1.''' Women in general; the female sex; the females collectively of the human kind.
{{smaller block|O despiteful love! unconstant ''womankind!''{{right|''Shak.'', T. of the S., iv. 2. 14.}}}}
{{smaller block|Teach ''Woman-kind'' Inconstancy and Pride.{{right|''Cowley'', The Mistress, Prophet.}}}}
{{smaller block|“Sair droukit was she, puir thing, sae I e’en put a glass o’ sherry in her water-gruel.” “Right, Grizel, right—let ''womankind'' alone for coddling each other.”{{right|''Scott'', Antiquary, ix.}}}}
'''2.''' A body of women, especially in a household; the female members of a family. [Humorous.]
{{smaller block|At last the Squire gracefully allowed the departure of his ''womenkind'', who floated away like a flock of released birds.{{right|''Mrs. Craik'', Agatha’s Husband, xv.}}}}

'''womanless''' (wu̇m′an-les), ''a.''   [< ''woman'' + ''-less''.]   Destitute of women.

'''womanlike''' (wu̇m′an-līk), ''a.'' Like a woman; womanly.
{{smaller block|''Womanlike'', taking revenge too deep for a transient wrong.{{right|''Tennyson'', Maud, iii.}}}}

'''womanliness''' (wu̇m′an-li-nes), ''n.'' The character of being womanly.
{{smaller block|There is nothyng wherein theyr ''womanlynesse'' is more honestely garnyshed than with sylence.{{right|''J. Udall'', On 1 Tim. ii.}}}}

'''womanly''' (wu̇m′an-li), ''a.''   [< ME. ''wommanlich'', ''wummonlich''; < ''woman'' + ''-ly''<sup>1</sup>.]   Characteristic of, like, or befitting a woman; suiting a woman; feminine; not masculine; not girlish: as, ''womanly'' behavior. {{smaller block|<poem>Thus muche as now, O ''womanliche'' wyf,
I may out bringe.</poem>{{right|''Chaucer'', Troilus, iii. 106.}}}}
{{smaller block|See where she comes, and brings your froward wives As prisoners to her ''womanly'' persuasion.{{right|''Shak.'', T. of the S., v. 2. 120.}}}}
{{smaller block|So that, loathed by their husbands and burning with a ''womanly'' spleen, in one night they [the women] massacred them all, together with their concubines.{{right|''Sandys'', Travailes, p. 19.}}}}
{{smaller block|A blushing ''womanly'' discovering grace.{{right|''Donne'', Elegy on his Mistress.}}}}
{{smaller block|Will she grow gentler, sweeter, more ''womanly?''{{right|''W. Black.''}}}}
='''Syn.''' ''Womanish'', ''Ladylike'', etc. See ''feminine''.

'''womanly''' (wu̇m′ạn-li), ''adv.''   [< ''womanly'', ''a.'']   In the manner of a woman.
{{smaller block|<poem>Lullaby can I sing too,
As ''womanly'' as can the best.</poem>{{right|''Gascoigne'', Lullabie of a Lover.}}}}

'''woman-post†''' (wu̇m′ạn-pōst), ''n.'' A female post or messenger. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|But who comes in such haste in riding-robes? What ''woman-post'' is this?
{{right|''Shak.'', K. John, i. 1. 218.}}}}

'''woman-queller''' (wu̇m′ạn-kwel″ėr), ''n.'' One who kills women. See ''manqueller''.
{{smaller block|Thou art a honey-seed, a man-queller, and a ''woman-queller.''{{right|''Shak.'', 2 Hen. IV., ii. 1. 58.}}}}

'''woman-suffrage''' (wu̇m′ạn-suf″rạ̄j), ''n.'' The exercise of the electoral franchise by women. [Colloq.]

'''woman-suffragist''' (wu̇m′ạn-suf″rā-jist), ''n.'' An advocate of woman-suffrage. [Colloq.]

'''woman-tired†''' (wu̇m′an-tīrd), ''a.''   [< ''woman'' + ''tired'', pp. of ''tire''<sup>2</sup>.]   Henpecked. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|<poem>Dotard! thou art ''woman-tired'', unroosted
By thy dame Partlet here. {{right|''Shak.'', W. T., ii. 3. 74.}}</poem>}}

'''woman-vested''' (wu̇m′an-ves″ted), ''a.'' Clothed like a woman; wearing women’s apparel. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|''Woman-vested'' as I was. {{right|''Tennyson'', Princess, iv.}}}}

'''womb''' (wöm), ''n.''   [E. dial. and Sc. ''wame''; < ME. ''wambe'', ''wombe'', < AS. ''wamb'', ''womb'', the belly, = OS. ''wamba'' = OFries. ''wamme'' = D. ''wam'', belly of a fish, = OHG. ''wamba'', ''wampa'' (''womba'', ''wumba''), MHG. ''wambe'', ''wampe'', later ''wamme'', G. ''wamme'', ''wampe'', belly, lap, = Icel. ''vömb'', belly, esp. of a beast, = Sw. ''våm'' = Dan. ''vom'' = Goth. ''wamba'', belly.]   '''1†.''' The belly; the stomach.
{{smaller block|<poem>Mete unto ''wombe'' and ''wombe'' eek unto mete,
Shal God destroyen bothe, as Paulus seith.
{{right|''Chaucer'', Pardoner’s Tale, l. 60.}}</poem>}}
{{smaller block|<poem>“Man, loue thi ''wombe'',” quod Gloteny.
{{right|''Hymns to Virgin'', etc. (E. E. T. S.), p. 64.}}</poem>}}
{{smaller block|An I had but a belly of any indifferency, I were simply the most active fellow in Europe. My ''womb'', my ''womb'', my ''womb'' undoes me. {{right|''Shak.'', 2 Hen. IV., iv. 3. 25.}}}}
{{smaller block|“Why, Andrew, you know all the secrets of the family.” “If I ken them, I can keep them,” said Andrew; “they winna work in my ''wame'' like barm in a barrel, I’se warrant ye.” {{right|''Scott'', Rob Roy, vi.}}}}
'''2.''' The uterus; the hollow dilated musculomembranous part of the female passages, between the vagina and the Fallopian tubes, in which the ovum is received, detained, and nourished during gestation, or the period intervening between fecundation and parturition: applied chiefly to this organ of the human female and some of the higher or better-known mammalian quadrupeds, the corresponding part of the passages of other animals being commonly called by the technical name ''uterus.'' See ''uterus'' (with cut), and cut under ''peritoneum.''
{{smaller block|That was Sein Johan, in his moder ''wombe.''
{{right|''Ancren Riwle'', I. 78.}}}}
{{smaller block|Twinn’d brothers of one ''womb.'' {{right|''Shak.'', T. of A., iv. 3. 3.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Ere the sad fruit of thy unhappy ''womb''
Had caus’d such sorrows past, and woes to come.</poem>
{{right|''Pope'', Iliad, xviii. 113.}}}}

Hence—'''3.''' The place where anything is produced.
{{smaller block|<poem>That did my ripe thoughts in my brain inhearse,
Making their tomb the ''womb'' wherein they grew.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Sonnets, lxxxvi.}}}}
{{smaller block|The ''womb'' of earth the genial seed receives.
{{right|''Dryden'', Georgics, ii. 439.}}}}

'''4.''' Any large or deep cavity that receives or contains anything.
{{smaller block|The fatal cannon’s ''womb.'' {{right|''Shak.'', R. and J., v. 1. 65.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>As, when black tempests mix the seas and skies,
The roaring deeps in wat’ry mountains rise,
Above the sides of some tall ship ascend,
Its ''womb'' they deluge, and its ribs they rend.</poem>
{{right|''Pope'', Iliad, xv. 443.}}}}
{{smaller block|'''Body of the womb.''' Same as ''corpus uteri'' (which see, under ''corpus'').—'''Falling of the womb.''' Same as ''prolapse of the uterus'' (which see, under ''uterus'').—'''Fundus of the womb,''' the upper part of the uterus.—'''Male womb.''' Same as ''prostatic vesicle'' (which see, under ''prostatic'').—'''Neck of the womb.''' Same as ''cervix uteri'' (which see, under ''cervix'').—'''Prolapse of the womb.''' Same as ''prolapse of the uterus'' (which see, under ''uterus'').}}

'''womb†''' (wöm), ''v. t.''   [< ''womb'', ''n.'']   To inclose; contain; breed in secret.
{{smaller block|<poem>Not . . . for all the sun sees or
The close earth ''wombs'' or the profound seas hide
In unknown fathoms, will I break my oath.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', W. T., iv. 4. 501.}}}}

'''wombat''' (wom′bat), ''n.''   [A corruption of the native Australian name ''womback'' or ''wombach.'']   An Australian marsupial mammal of the genus ''Phascolomys'', as ''P. wombat'' or ''P. ursinus.'' See cut under ''Phascolomys.''

'''womb-brother†''' (wöm′bruᴛ̵ʜ″ėr), ''n.'' A brother uterine. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|Edmund of Haddam . . . was son to Queen Katherine by Owen Theodor, her second husband, ''Womb-brother'' to King Henry the Sixth, and Father to King Henry the Seventh.
{{right|''Fuller'', Worthies. (''Davies.'')}}}}

'''wombed''' (wömd), ''a.''   [< ''womb'' + ''-ed''<sup>2</sup>.]   Having a womb, in any sense.
{{smaller block|<poem>I’ll muster forces, an unvanquish’d power;
Cornets of horse shall press th’ ungrateful earth;
This hollow ''wombed'' mass shall inly groan,
And murmur to sustain the weight of arms.</poem>
{{right|''Marston'', Antonio and Mellida, I., iii. 1.}}}}

'''womb-grain''' (wöm′grān), ''n.'' Ergot, or spurred rye (technically called ''secale cornutum''): so called from the effect of the drug upon the uterus.

'''womb-passage''' (wöm′pas″ạ̄j), ''n.'' The vagina. See cut under ''peritoneum.''

'''womb-pipe†''', ''n.'' Same as ''womb-passage.''   ''Cotgrave.''<noinclude><references/></noinclude>
